about: Andoverpis (Antwerp) on the Scheldt, 793 to 1066: a church, a toll and a landing on a sand rise that becomes a walled castle of the eastern kingdom. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/andoverpis.md and the spine (threads dorestad_falls, book_road, hungry_years; cast.alcuin, cast.hamacar, cast.gerlef, cast.thiadbod, cast.rorik, cast.rollo). A draft for the user to overwrite. Read the note first.
note: In 793 the digs show no fort here: ploughland, a post-built house, a stake pen, and a church and a toll known only from the charter of 726. So the place begins as a hamlet and grows by eras: close-set houses after 850, a turf rampart about 900, the march about 974 to 980, oak piles and perhaps stone after 1007. No lay person is named here between 793 and 1008, so every person but the margrave is ours, and each says so in its source. Where the church stood is not known; the game puts it on the rise east of the landing and says so. No market or mint is on record before 1066: 'the selling bank' is our name for the ground where goods change hands off the boats. The giant, the hand and the stone castle of the later town are not of these years and are not here.

ports.summary: Andoverpis in 793 is a church, a toll and a landing on a sand rise where the Schijn runs into the Scheldt: a few timber houses among fields, a point of firm ground called the werf where boats lie, and a river that turns twice a day. A merchant comes for pork, hides and antler combs at the maker's price, for the ferry north, and for a quiet tide on the way between the sea and the abbeys at Ganda. It is small, and it is the only place on this reach where somebody takes the toll by an old right and can show the leaf that says so.
ports.seasons: The river is tidal and grey-brown, and the flats flood from midwinter to Lent, so boats come between Easter and Martinmas. The comb-maker comes with the swallows and leaves at Martinmas; pigs are driven in from the mast woods and killed before Advent; salt comes up from the islands in autumn. The feast of the church is Peter and Paul, in the week after Saint John's day, and Saint Amand is kept in the dead of winter.

history.text: About this year Eligius, bishop of Noyon, preaches at Andoverpis and turns the Suevi there from their errors. It is the oldest writing of the name.
history.source: Life of Eligius, as printed in Mertens and Torfs, Geschiedenis van Antwerpen I (1845): 'jugi instantia Andoverpis decertavit, et multis erroribus implicatos Suevos convertit'; nl.wikipedia Geschiedenis van Antwerpen (dossier 3, 6)

history.text: About this year the moneyer Chrodigisilus strikes small gold pieces with the name ANDERPVS. No coin is known from the place in the game's years.

On the twentieth day of October Rauchingus and his wife Bebelina give Willibrord the church of Saint Peter and Saint Paul, built by Amandus within the castrum Antwerpis, with a third of the toll, for incense and lights and for the priests' prayers. Rauchingus had the church by exchange from Abbot Firminus for his hamlet Tumme.
history.source: The charter of 20 October 726, in Dutch in Mertens and Torfs I (1845), pp. 74-75 (the Latin not read: Wampach, Echternach no. 34 (?)); nl.wikipedia Rauchingus

history.text: This year there is famine across the Frankish lands. The digs show Andoverpis as ploughland on a sand rise with the first timber buildings going up: a house on deep posts, stake fences, a round pen. No rampart and no wall.
At Thionville the emperor rules that only old and just tolls may be taken. The toll here was already taken in 726.
history.source: chronicle_793.json (Thionville 805); the charter of 726 in Mertens and Torfs I

history.text: On the twenty-eighth day of December (or in 808) a great flood is written down at Saint-Amand, up the Scheldt.

This year the Northmen burned the town of Andwerpa, and likewise Witla, the trading place by the mouth of the Maas, and took tribute from the Frisians. No leader is named, and no burnt layer has been tied to it.
history.source: Annales Fuldenses 836: 'Nordmanni Andwerpam civitatem incendunt, similiter et Witlam emporium iuxta ostium Mosae fluminis, et a Frisionibus tributum acceperunt' (our rendering). The game's chronicle entry 836-witla-antwerp-burned cites the Annals of Saint-Bertin, which do not have it

history.text: The Northmen take Walcheren at the river's mouth and kill its count. In 841 the emperor Lothar gives the island to the Dane Harald.
At Verdun the brothers share the kingdom. The Scheldt becomes a border: the right bank, and Andoverpis with it, is Lothar's.
From about this year the first close-set houses stand side by side on sill beams, five to six metres wide, some built of timber used before. The oldest had ship's timber in them.
history.source: Bellens 2021 (houses A, B, C; Van de Walle's note on reused ship's timber) (dossier 2)

history.text: In November the great army crosses from England, winters at Ghent and raids the Scheldt for a year.

About this year a palisade, and then a bank of turves and spoil thirteen and a half metres wide, is thrown up in a half ring open to the river. Leather is worked inside it; paths of split logs run along its foot.
Between 923 and 927 Andoverpis, chief place of the land of Rien, passes to the eastern kingdom. The river is the border with the count of Flanders.
history.source: nl.wikipedia Geschiedenis van Antwerpen; nl.wikipedia Land van Rijen (dossier 5)

history.text: Between about 974 and 980 the emperor makes a march of the place against Flanders. The date is not settled. Godfrey of Verdun is listed, with reserve, as its first margrave.
history.source: Bellens 2021; en.wikipedia Het Steen; nl.wikipedia Markgraafschap Antwerpen (dossier 3, 5)

history.text: A charter names 'the county of Count Gozilo, which is called Antwerf'. Gothelo is margrave from 1005 or 1008. Between 1007 and 1015 oak piles are driven along the castle's edge.
history.source: The charter of 1008 in Mertens and Torfs I (1845); en.wikipedia Gothelo I of Lorraine; Bellens 2021 (tree-ring dates of the piles)

history.text: Baldwin, count of Flanders, takes the march in his war with the emperor, and in 1049 gives it up.
This year the Flemings besiege Duke Frederick in the castle, fail to take it, and burn the houses that stand round it.
history.source: Mertens and Torfs I (1845), p. 135, after Sigebert's chronicle (not read in Latin); Bellens 2021 (dossier 5)

eras.text: King Charles's years and his son's. A hamlet on a sand rise: the church of Peter and Paul, a toll taken at the werf, one big house on posts where ale is brewed, a round pen, pigs. The first two summers are hungry. A Frisian comb-maker works under a lean-to from spring to Martinmas, and Rhenish pots come down in every boat.

The year it burned, and after. Black posts and a toll nobody takes for a season; then new sills laid on the old ground, with timber from a boat nobody came back for. Danes hold Walcheren at the river's mouth from 841 and every ship from the sea has passed them.

Houses stand close, side by side, short end to the path. The river is the border between two kings. In 879 and 880 the great army sits at Ghent, a tide and a half upstream, and the stock is kept inland again. Graves are dug on the rise east of the houses.

A bank of turves in a half ring, open to the water, with a palisade under it and log paths along its foot. Inside: long narrow plots, wattle houses with ash on the floors, stables, a smith, leather on every fence. White pots from the Maas outnumber the red-painted ones from the Rhine. From about 925 the lord is the eastern king's.

A march of the empire against Flanders: a margrave's timber hall, a toll house, armed men at the bank. Dwellings stand where the stables were, and houses have spilled outside the bank. Sea fish begins to be eaten.

Count Gothelo's years. Oak piles are driven along the castle's edge and stone from Tournai comes down the river by the bargeload; a chapel of Saint Walburga stands in the middle. The name is said Antwerf.

Flanders wants the march. Baldwin holds it for two years and gives it back; in 1055 his men come again, cannot take the castle and burn every house outside it. Those are built again within the year. Saint Michael's, south of the castle, is the mother church, with twelve canons.

sites.name: The werf
sites.see: A blunt point of firm sand pushed out into a wide grey-brown river, with three or four boats grounded along it and mud shining on either side where the inlets cut back. Behind, a low rise with thatch and one thread of smoke; across the water, a flat green line and nothing. The tide sucks at the stakes, a pig squeals somewhere inland, and the air is river mud and peat smoke.
sites.source: Bellens 2021: the ragged bank of points and inlets, the chief point the werf; stakes and jetties are his supposition, none were dug. The tide range of 2.5 to 3.5 m is a guess (Research/water_levels/north_sea_core.md)

sites.name: The toll post
sites.see: A squared oak post at the head of the werf with notches cut down one side, and a bench under a hide awning where a man sits with a tally stick and a small scale. Every path up from the boats passes his knee. In the later years the bench is a timber toll house inside the bank, with a shuttered window on the landing.
sites.source: The toll is in the charter of 726, a third of it the church's (Mertens and Torfs I, 1845). The post and bench are ours. A toll house in the castle: Inventaris Onroerend Erfgoed, Het Steen (date not given)

sites.name: Saint Peter and Saint Paul
sites.see: A small timber church with a shingled roof on the highest of the sand, its west door facing the river and a wooden cross by the path. Inside it is dark and smells of tallow and a little old incense; two lamps hang before the altar and one is not lit. A chest with an iron hasp stands against the north wall.
sites.source: The church built by Amandus and given to Willibrord in 726, for incense and lights (Mertens and Torfs I). Its site is unknown: guesses are the later castle, the Koraalberg or under Saint Michael's (Bellens 2021). That it is of timber and stands on the rise is ours

sites.name: The comb-maker's lean-to
sites.see: A lean-to of hurdles against the big house's south wall, open to the light. Stag skulls with the antlers still on them hang by their eye-holes from a rail; under them a man sits astride a bench with a fine saw, and the ground round his feet is white with chips and dust. Finished combs lie in a row on a board, teeth up, and it smells of scorched bone.
sites.source: Bellens 2021: 18 combs, 13 pin beaters, 11 whorls, and the whole chain of work from sawn stag skulls to finished comb, beginning before the rampart; the makers perhaps travelling men. The lean-to is ours

sites.name: The selling bank
sites.see: The trodden ground between the werf and the first fence. Crates of grey Rhenish pots packed in straw stand open by a boat's bow; a woman holds two piglets by the hind legs; hides are pegged out, hair down, and somebody is always arguing over a measure of rye. There are no booths. When the tide makes, the boats lift and half the sellers go with them.
sites.source: No market is recorded before 1066 (dossier 8): this is where goods change hands, and the name is ours. Goods from Bellens 2021: Badorf ware and relief-band amphorae about 793; pork, old plough oxen, sheep, rye, wheat and barley from the back country

sites.name: The house on posts
sites.see: The biggest roof in the place: a long timber house with two great posts at its middle and a door wide enough for a cask. One wall plank is curved, with a row of old rivet holes along it. Inside, a fire on the floor, benches, a vat under a cloth, and split tally sticks hanging in bunches from a rafter. It smells of malt, smoke and wet wool. This is the ale-house; in later years it is one of a row.
sites.source: Bellens 2021: a post-built house of 770-900 on the south plot, two deep posts and stake rows; reused ship's timber in the oldest houses (Van de Walle). That ale is brewed and sold in it is ours

sites.name: The Schijn ferry
sites.see: North of the houses the land drops to peat and reed, and a brown creek mouth as wide as a bowshot opens into the river. A flat boat lies on a rope between two posts; on the far side a track goes off north through the wet toward Merksem. Curlews, and the ferryman's dog asleep on the landing.
sites.source: A ferry crossed the mouth of the Schijn at Dambrugge toward Merksem; later it was the abbey of Lobbes's (?) (nl.wikipedia Geschiedenis van Antwerpen; dossier 1). The low peat of the Schijn delta: Bellens 2021

sites.name: The pen and the dark fields
sites.see: Strips of grey-black ploughland run back from the houses, and broken red potsherds turn up in every furrow. At the field's edge stands a round pen of thirty pointed stakes, hardly wider than a man is tall twice over, with a sow and her young in it. Open country beyond: meadow, few trees, a boy with a stick.
sites.source: Bellens 2021: the dark layer of grey sand full of worn Roman sherds, worked from Roman times into the early 9th century; a round pen just under 4 m across of some thirty pointed stakes, 770-900; pig bones 46 in a hundred

sites.name: The graves on the rise
sites.see: A hump of sand east of the houses with a few low mounds on it, each with a post at the head, and one small roof on four posts over nothing in particular. From here the whole place can be seen at once: roofs, the werf, the river bending away south. Wind in dry grass.
sites.source: Bellens 2021: two burials of the 9th century on the Koraalberg, probably more, perhaps a chapel (his proposal); outside the later rampart

sites.name: The south inlet
sites.see: A muddy cut running back from the river beside the werf, dry at half ebb. A small boat lies on her side on rollers with two strakes off; a man with an adze works at a plank laid over trestles, and old ship's timbers are stacked under a hurdle to be used again. Wood chips, the knock of a mallet, a pot of tar warming.
sites.source: Bellens 2021: the inlets between the points are the later town ditches (ruien); carpenters, and ship's timber reused in houses. No ship or yard has been found: the yard is ours

sites.name: The bank and the log paths
sites.see: A grass bank twice a man's height and as wide as a house is long, curving from the river round the houses and back to the river, with a row of posts along its crest. At its inner foot a path of split logs runs dry over the mud; a smith's hammer rings somewhere behind the wattle and hides hang on the fences. After the year 1000 grey stone begins to stand along its outer face.
sites.source: Bellens 2021: post rows, then a bank of turves and spoil 13.5 m wide, D-shaped and open to the river, still 4 m high in 1887; corduroy paths 1.5 m and 1 m wide; over 12 kg of smith's slag; leather work after the rampart. Stone: oak piles felled 1007-1015 at the wall's foot (Bellens; Inventaris Onroerend Erfgoed, Burchtzone)

sites.name: The margrave's hall
sites.see: A long timber hall in the middle of the ground inside the bank, its door posts carved, shields on the wall inside and a high seat at the far end under a hanging. Armed men lounge at the door; a clerk with a wax board sits by the hearth. Close by stands a small chapel of Saint Walburga, whom sailors call on in storms.
sites.source: A toll house, a mint house and the margrave's timber hall in the castle, date not given (Inventaris Onroerend Erfgoed, Het Steen); Saint Walburga's chapel mid-castle, probably 11th century (Bellens 2021); Walburga and sailors (en.wikipedia Saint Walpurga). The game shows no mint: none is known before 1066

people.name: Adalwin
people.trait: Holds out an open hand before he says a word, and counts aloud so nobody can say he counted wrong.
people.want: The king's two thirds and the church's third to come out even on the stick before any king's man asks.
people.fear: A stranger with a wax board asking by what right a toll is taken on this bank.
people.voice: Slow, exact, fond of the word 'old'. Says a number, then says it again.
people.looks: Forty-five in 793, broad and short, cropped grey hair, a brown tunic belted high, leg bands, a long notched tally stick in one hand and the other hand open.
knows: the toll here and what the leaf of 726 says of it, by heart, though he cannot read
which boats have gone up to Ganda this moon and what they sat deep with
the new penny and the old, and that he may not refuse a good one
the turn of the tide at the werf, to the length of a psalm

ties.note: The priest has a third of the toll and counts the boats himself from the church door.
Drinks at her fire every evening and tells her what came in; she tells him what he missed.
The toll man at the Maas mouth; they send word of bad payers by any skipper going that way.
The abbey cellarer up river sends his boats past with a blessing and a claim that Saint Bavo pays no toll.
The king's steward on Walichrum is the nearest man who can ask him for an account.
Thiadbod gave him a good cloak one Easter, and has paid on a light count ever since.
The comb-maker says a comb made and sold on this bank owes nothing. Adalwin says the stag was not born on this bank. They have it out every Martinmas.
The wright up river sends for oak by the raft and thinks the emperor's name on an order is a toll charter. It is not. Adalwin counts the rafts aloud.
The stone dealer of Colonia sends querns up to the abbeys and grudges the tenth in stones; Adalwin has a stack of black querns by the post and no mill.

lines.greet: Hand first, talk after. One part in ten of what you sell on this bank. Two thirds to the lord king, one third to Saint Peter.
lines.greet_again: You again. Same boat, deeper in the water. Good. That is more for the king and more for the saint.
rumour: The Frisian under the lean-to wants stag heads. He will give a dozen combs for a bundle and call it a bargain for you.
They say the lord king has made the penny heavier. I have weighed three. They are heavier. I say it again: heavier.
lines.saying: This toll is old. Old as the church. A new toll is a robbery; an old one is the weather.
lines.old_toll: Since the law of Thionville men ask if my toll is old. I send them up to the church. The leaf is in the chest.
lines.hand: A man who swears falsely to me loses the hand he swore with. That is the lord king's law, not my joke.
lines.farewell: Go down on the ebb and keep the right bank. And tell them at the Maas mouth that Adalwin counts everything.

people.source: invented; the toll and its thirds from the charter of 726 (Mertens and Torfs I, 1845); only old tolls lawful from 805 (chronicle_793.json); 'shall lose his right hand' of a perjurer, capitulary of 802 c. 36 (Henderson 1892, as given in peoples/frankish.md 3)

people.name: Hildulf
people.trait: A priest alone in a small church who was schooled in a great abbey and has not forgiven the difference.
people.want: A book of his own to read from on Saint Willibrord's day; both lamps lit; somebody to speak Latin with.
people.fear: That the abbey has forgotten it owns this church, and that he will die here unvisited.
people.voice: Dry, learned, a little hungry. Names the saint whose day it is before he says good morning.
people.looks: Thin, about forty, tonsured, a patched black-brown tunic to the ankle, ink on two fingers, a small iron key on a thong round his neck.
knows: what the charter of 726 gives the church, and the curse at the end of it, word for word
the feasts and fasts, and which day a boat may not be loaded
who is hungry in the houses and who is only saying so
that Abbot Beornrad of Echternach is kin to Alcuin, and that a Life of Willibrord has been written
Latin, and enough letters to read a leaf for a merchant

ties.note: Counts the boats from the church door and compares his count with the toll man's stick at Michaelmas.
She feeds him in Lent on credit and has never cut a stick for it.
Heard Alcuin teach once at Echternach when the master visited his kinsman the abbot (?); has lived on it since.
Willibrord's other house at Traiectum is the nearest place with a school and a book to copy from.
They write to each other when a boat goes; the schoolmaster answers one letter in three.
The scribe at Saint Bavo up river lends him a quire to copy when a boat is going, and wants it back by the next.
The priest at the Maas mouth; they share one copy of the feasts and argue about Easter.
A bishop's clerk at Colonia has offered the carrier four times his thirty pennies for the same Life of Willibrord. Hildulf has never seen the man and prays for him by name, with an effort.

lines.greet: Peter and Paul keep you. The church has a third of what you just paid, so you are already a benefactor. Come in.
lines.greet_again: You came back. The second lamp is still dark. I mention it only because you asked how I was.
rumour: The grain in the far strips stood tall at Pentecost and there was nothing in the ear. I touched it. I will not say what I thought.
The leaf in my chest curses whoever takes this church's goods: the lot of Judas and the leprosy of Gehazi. The toll man knows it by heart.
lines.saying: Incense and lights, the giver wrote. He did not write who pays for them now.
lines.book: A Life of our Willibrord has been written, in good Latin. They have it at Traiectum. I have a chest and no book to put in it.
lines.eligius: Bishop Eligius strove here without rest, the Life says. It does not say he enjoyed it.
lines.farewell: Go with God. If you pass Traiectum, greet the schoolmaster, and ask him what a copy costs. Do not tell him I asked twice.

people.source: invented; the church, its third of the toll, the incense and lights and the curse from the charter of 726 (Mertens and Torfs I, 1845); Beornrad, abbot of Echternach 775-797 and Alcuin's cousin (en.wikipedia Beornrad); Alcuin's Life of Willibrord, written for Beornrad before 797 (?); whether Echternach still held the church in 793 is unchecked (?); 'jugi instantia Andoverpis decertavit' (Life of Eligius, Latin, our rendering); the false grain of 793 (chronicle_793.json 793-spring-false-grain)

people.name: Liafgrim
people.trait: A travelling comb-maker who comes with the swallows and goes at Martinmas, and judges every man by his hair.
people.want: Good stag antler, shed or cut, more than this country's hunters bring him; and a pupil with steady hands.
people.fear: His eyes, and the dust in his chest that makes him cough each spring a little longer.
people.voice: Dry, quick, never looks up from the saw. Prices everything in combs.
people.looks: Lean, in his thirties in 793, fair hair combed flat and tied, a Frisian short cloak pinned on the right shoulder, white bone dust to the elbows, a fine saw in his fist.
knows: antler: which tine makes teeth and which makes plates, and what a bundle is worth here and in the north
what combs fetch at Walichrum, at Dorestad and among the Danes, a season old
the creeks between the Scheldt and the Maas, because he rows them twice a year
every ale-house from here to the Vlie and what is owed in each

ties.note: Lodges against her wall and pays in combs and pins; she says the stick is longer than he thinks.
Argues every year that a comb made on this bank and sold on this bank owes nothing.
The brooch-maker on the island; they winter at the same hearth and swap rivets for offcuts.
Thiadbod's men try to buy his whole summer at once, at a price for the lot.
Has sold combs to Northmen at the sea markets and likes how they pay: by weight, without talk.
The only smith on the Rhine whose saw holds its set in stag antler. A new blade comes down each spring by any boat; a comb goes back, and Liafgrim wonders who wears it.

lines.greet: You have a seaman's hair. Salt and knots. Sit there, out of my light. Did you bring antler?
lines.greet_again: The same head, a little greyer. Mine too. What did you bring me this time?
rumour: The Danes pay double for a comb with a case. They will not be seen with lice. I respect that in a people.
On Walichrum they found old pennies in the sand again. Wilbraht melts them for pins and tells the steward nothing.
lines.saying: A comb has two rows of teeth and no appetite. I know lords of whom I cannot say as much.
lines.work: Three days to a comb if nobody talks to me. Five if the priest comes. He wants to know what it means.
lines.pupil: Your boy has still hands. Leave him with me a summer. I will send back a comb-maker or a boy who hates bone.
lines.farewell: If you go north, bring stag. Not elk, not ox horn. Stag. I can tell with my eyes shut.

people.source: invented; the comb work and its waste from Bellens 2021 (antler workers 'perhaps travelling men'); Frisians living here are not attested after the 7th century (dossier 8), so he is a visitor; the short cloak from Notker I.34 (Grant 1905, peoples/frankish.md)

people.name: Ermentrud
people.trait: Keeps the house on posts and a split stick for every man who ever drank in it. Forgets nothing and says so kindly.
people.want: Malt in a hungry year; her daughter's child to grow up knowing the sticks; the roof made good before winter.
people.fear: Fire in the thatch, and a year with no boats.
people.voice: Warm and exact. Calls a skipper by his father's name until he has earned his own.
people.looks: A big woman past forty, grey-brown hair under a linen cloth, sleeves rolled, a wooden ladle in her belt and a bunch of tally sticks on a cord at her hip.
knows: who is in the place tonight, who left on the ebb, and who owes whom
what you drank last time, what you said, and what you promised
the price of pigs, rye and malt in the back country this moon
that the curved plank in her wall came off a boat, and whose boat

ties.note: Her daughter's daughter, born about 812, who will have the house and the sticks after her.
He tells her what came in; she tells him who slipped past at dusk. Neither calls it informing.
Feeds him in Lent and takes his blessing on the vat as payment.
He lodges against her wall; she has more combs than any woman on the river.
The ale-wife at Ganda sends down skippers who pay, with a knot in a cord to say so.
The ale-wife on the island; skippers carry each one's opinion of the other's brewing up and down the river.
The pilot of the Maas mouth brought her husband's boat home without him, and would take nothing for it.
Her cups and her spouted pots are the Colonia widow's, known by the mark under the handle. They have never met; each has asked a skipper what the other looks like.
The king's steward at Colonia promised barley for this bank in the hungry spring and it came a week late. She brewed thin and told every skipper whose boat it was not.

lines.greet: A new face. Whose son are you? Sit by the fire. The first cup is for the house's luck; the second goes on a stick.
lines.greet_again: There you are. You had the bench by the post and you owe me for three. I kept the stick. I keep them all.
rumour: No malt to be had above the price of silver. I am brewing thin and saying so. Bring barley and name your own bench.
A boat of poor people came down from the south at dusk, asking where there is bread. I gave them broth. There is no bread.
lines.saying: The river brings everybody back. That is why I never throw a stick away.
lines.plank: That plank was my man's boat. The river kept him and sent her home. So she holds the wall up. Somebody should.
lines.trust: You paid when you could have sailed. I saw. Leave your casks in my loft; nobody will touch them while I breathe.
lines.farewell: Go safely. Come back before Martinmas and I will have killed a pig. Come after and I will have eaten it.

people.source: invented; the post-built house and the reused ship's timber from Bellens 2021; the famine of 792-794 from chronicle_793.json and the spine thread hungry_years (the boat of people who have left a famine village)

people.name: Ansgard
people.trait: Ermentrud's granddaughter: counted the sails in the year of the fire and has counted every sail since.
people.want: The house up again on the old sills; the sticks kept dry; never again to be the last to know.
people.fear: Smoke down river in a dry summer.
people.voice: Short and level. Says what she saw and how many, and stops.
people.looks: Fourteen in 826, a woman of twenty-four in the year of the fire and old after it: dark hair cut to the neck, a burn scar on the left forearm, her grandmother's sticks at her belt, some of them charred at one end.
knows: how many ships came in 836, from which bank, and how long the place burned
the high ground inland where pigs and children can be hidden in a morning
what the Danes on Walichrum ask of a boat going to sea, this year
every debt her grandmother's sticks still carry, and which house's heir stands before her

ties.note: Her mother's mother; she carried the tally sticks out of the house before anything else.
Her daughter's son, born about 868, who will build where she rebuilt.
The count of the island came up river to count spears in the years before the fire. He counted eleven.
The salter sells her salt for salt pork, and sends word up with the salt when the lords of the island change.
From 841 every boat that reaches her from the sea has paid the Dane something first.
She will not have the name spoken at her fire. Skippers who sail under his peace drink there all the same.

lines.greet: You are of the house that had the bench by the post. I have your stick. Sit. Tell me what you saw at the river mouth.
lines.greet_again: You. Good. How many sails between here and the sea, and whose? Drink after.
rumour: Dorestat was plundered at midsummer. A man who swam for it told me at this fire. I have sent the sows inland.
The Danes on Walichrum take a cask from every wine boat and call it a gift. The skippers call it cheaper than burning.
lines.saying: Smoke goes up, word goes down river. I trust the smoke.
lines.fire: They came on the flood, in the morning. I counted nine ships and stopped. The church went first. It was the driest.
lines.after: The new wall has a boat in it again. Nobody came back for her. In this place the river always pays for the timber.
lines.farewell: Go down on the ebb and look behind you at the bend. If you see smoke here, do not come back for your casks.

people.source: invented; the burning from Annales Fuldenses 836 (no leader named, and what burned is not known: that the church burned is tradition (nl.wikipedia Sint-Walburgiskerk) and our choice); Dorestad plundered 834-836 (Annales Bertiniani); Walcheren given to Harald in 841 (Annales Bertiniani). That Rorik or Harald ruled the Scheldt is unsourced (dossier 8), and she does not say they do

people.name: Hartbert
people.trait: A carpenter who builds boats when there is oak and houses when there is not, and set the post rows under the bank.
people.want: Straight oak, more than the open country here grows; and the bank finished before the next fleet, not after.
people.fear: That the bank will be tried before the turf has knit.
people.voice: Measures as he talks, in feet and hand-spans. Speaks of timber as if it had a temper.
people.looks: Broad in the shoulder, thirty in 898, sandy beard, a leather apron over a short tunic, an adze through his belt and a knotted measuring cord round his neck.
knows: every plank in the place that has been a boat, and what boat
what the bank is made of and where it is still soft
the price of oak at Ganda and on the Maas, and who will float it down
what a hull needs before she goes to sea, and what she can do without

ties.note: His mother's mother; he learned to count on her tally sticks.
The line goes on from him: Gerburg is his son's son's daughter, and keeps the sticks.
The countess across the river: her husband the count builds forts of his own and buys up the oak Hartbert wants (?).
Two of his best men went to the Seine, where a wright is paid in land. He has not replaced them.
The count of Flanders across the river builds forts at every river mouth and takes the straight oak for them; what reaches Hartbert is what the count's wrights turned down (?).

lines.greet: Mind the trestle. If you want a seam looked at, haul her up at half ebb. If you want oak, so do I.
lines.greet_again: Your boat is drier than last year. Somebody tarred her properly. Not me; I would remember the hull.
rumour: The bank is nine paces through at the foot. I paced it. Turf outside, spoil inside, and my posts under all of it.
They found an old bronze penny in the spoil with a king's head on it. Nobody knows the king. It went back in the bank.
lines.saying: A boat is a house that leaves. A house is a boat that learned sense.
lines.bank: Every householder owes a stretch of the bank. A stranger with a plot owes one too. That is how you stop being a stranger.
lines.timber: My great-grandmother's wall had a boat in it. So has mine. Bring me new oak and I will stop robbing the dead.
lines.farewell: Keep her bailed. And if you see straight oak lying idle anywhere on this river, I never asked whose it was.

people.source: invented; the palisade and bank of about 900, 13.5 m wide, and the long narrow plots from Bellens 2021; the Roman coin of Constans found in the rampart (Bellens); Meuse ware outweighing Rhenish in the 10th century (Bellens); Flanders builds forts in the 880s (realms/francia.md); Rollo at Rouen from 911 (spine). That householders owed a stretch of the bank is ours (?)

people.name: Gothelo
people.trait: The margrave: a lord of the eastern kingdom set on a river bank to watch Flanders, and later duke of all Lotharingia.
people.want: The toll counted, the wall finished in stone, and the count across the river kept across the river.
people.fear: A Flemish fleet on the flood while he is away at the emperor's court, which is most of the year.
people.voice: Brief, used to being obeyed, speaks of the emperor as 'my lord' and of merchants as weather: useful when it comes.
people.looks: A heavy man in his forties in 1008, grey later, a long dark-blue cloak with a gold pin, a sword with a silver-wound hilt, riding boots; seldom without a hound at his knee.
knows: what the emperor wants of this border, this year
which lords of Lotharingia are for the emperor and which are waiting
what stone from Tournai costs by the bargeload, because he pays for it
nothing about prices, and that his toll man does

ties.note: Her house sends ale to his hall at every feast; his men drink there when he is away, and pay.
The counts of Flanders want the right bank: Baldwin IV in his first years here and the fifth Baldwin after him. He was set on this bank to say no, in oak and then in stone.
The Count Palatine on the Rhine, an emperor's son-in-law: the other great house of Lotharingia, whose stretch of river he would gladly have (?).

lines.greet: You are the merchant with the charter. Show it to my clerk. If it is good you will find this a quiet river.
lines.greet_again: Your house again. My toll man speaks well of you, which costs you money, so I believe him.
rumour: The stone comes from Tournai, down my enemy's river, in my enemy's barges. He takes my silver for it. That is a border.
My lord the emperor keeps Easter far from here. I am to hold this bank until he remembers it. I have held it eleven years.
The Danish king holds England now, and keeps the sea quiet, I am told. A quiet sea brings Flemings up my river with full holds.
lines.saying: A wall is a letter to your neighbour. Mine is being written in stone so he can read it.
lines.wall: Oak piles first, then stone on them. A wright told me the old bank had boats in it. This one will have a quarry.
lines.farewell: Go. Pay at the toll house, not on the werf. A man who pays on the werf has paid somebody who is not me.

people.source: Gothelo I, about 967 to 19 April 1044, margrave of Antwerp from 1005 or 1008, duke of Lower Lotharingia from 1023 and of Upper from 1033 (en.wikipedia Gothelo I of Lorraine; nl.wikipedia Gozelo I van Lotharingen); the charter of 1008, 'the county of Count Gozilo, which is called Antwerf' (Mertens and Torfs I, 1845); oak piles of 1007-1015 and Tournai stone (Bellens 2021). No visit of his to the place is recorded: that a merchant finds him in his hall here is ours (?). The words are ours

people.name: Gerburg
people.trait: Keeps the old ale-house, which now stands outside the wall, and the oldest tally sticks on the river, some of them charred.
people.want: A plot inside the wall before the Flemings come again, and not to pay the margrave's price for it.
people.fear: That the house outside the wall will burn, as the sticks say it has before.
people.voice: Quick, amused, with her foremothers' habit of telling a guest what he owes before he sits.
people.looks: A spare woman, twenty-two in 1022 and white-haired by the siege, a blue wool gown with a woven band, a ring of keys and a bundle of very old sticks in a leather case at her belt.
knows: what your house owed and was owed here in her foremothers' time, by the oldest sticks
who holds which plot inside the wall and what he paid
when the margrave is away, and how many men he left
what English and Flemish pennies are taken for on this bank, this moon

ties.note: Her father's father's father; the house's long wall is still his work.
Sends ale to the hall at feasts, and hears there what the wall is costing.
Has never seen him: but in his years the sea was quiet and her box filled with his pennies, and she drinks to him yet.
The count of Flanders, whose men burn every roof outside the wall in 1055, hers first. She has sold ale to his bargemen for thirty years and will again.

lines.greet: I know your mark. It is on a stick older than this roof. Your people owed mine for three cups. Sit; we will call it even.
lines.greet_again: The house with the old stick. Welcome. Is it true what they say down river, or only loud?
rumour: The margrave is at the emperor's court again. He left twenty men and a clerk. The clerk is the dangerous one.
Stone for the wall came down from Tournai at Saint Peter's Chains. The bargemen were Flemings. They looked at the wall a long time.
lines.saying: Inside the wall you pay for the ground. Outside it you pay for the wall, when somebody comes to try it.
lines.sticks: This one is burnt at the end. That was the first fire, the heathen one. We carry the sticks out first. Always the sticks.
lines.after_siege: They could not take the castle, so they took my roof. It is up again. The sticks never left my belt.
lines.farewell: Go well. If you buy a plot, buy it inside. I say that as a woman who did not.

people.source: invented; houses outside the wall from the 10th century (Bellens 2021; Inventaris Onroerend Erfgoed, Burchtzone); sea fishing after 1000 (Bellens); the siege of 1055 and the burning of the houses round the castle (Mertens and Torfs I, p. 135, after Sigebert; Bellens); Cnut's peace 1016-1035 (spine thread price_of_england)

stories.title: The sticks first
stories.summary: From 834 the fleets that plunder Dorestad pass the river mouths every summer, and in 836 one of them comes up the Scheldt on the flood and burns Andoverpis in the same season as Witla. What the place saves depends on how early it hears, and a merchant is the fastest news on the river.
stories.picture: A morning flood on a wide brown river: long dark ships coming round the bend under oars, and on the sand rise a young woman running from a big thatched house with a bundle of tally sticks held to her chest, pigs scattering ahead of her.

beats.text: Ansgard asks every skipper the same thing: how many sails between here and the sea, and whose. The count of Walichrum has been up river and counted eleven spears. She wants to know what you saw at the Maas mouth.

She does not want comfort. She wants a number and a day. A skipper who tells her plainly that the fleets which took Dorestad pass the Scheldt mouth every summer, and that the flood would carry them here in one tide, has told her what the count of the island would not.

A tide and a half up river the canons of Saint Bavo's ask the same question more politely, and send to know what the ale-wife at Andoverpis has counted. They do not move their saint. Their own fire is fifteen years off, and they will be at Laon with the bones when it comes.

At Witla boats lie ready to run and stores go inland by the creeks. The pilot's people say a fleet does not need a pilot for the Scheldt: it is wide, and the flood carries a ship to Andoverpis in one tide.
From the island's dune every sail that turns into the Scheldt can be seen half a day before it reaches the werf. Somebody could carry that half day up river, if somebody were going.

This year the Northmen burn the place. If word came ahead of them the houses are empty, the pigs are in the woods and the church's chest is in a pit; if not, they take what stands. Either way the posts are black by evening.
New sills are laid on the old ground. A boat lies in the south inlet that nobody has come back for, and her strakes go into Ansgard's wall. She asks if you will stand the oak for the rest.

endings.how: Brought word up river from Walichrum or Witla before the fleet (the thread's flag df_warned).
endings.text: The houses burn empty. The sows, the children, the priest's chest and the sticks are a morning's walk inland. Ansgard cuts a new stick for your house and writes nothing on it: it is the only one she keeps that way.
endings.reward: Ansgard and her line fast friends of the house, carried to the heirs; free lodging and storage here for good; standing with the Franks of the Scheldt.

endings.how: Was not in time, but stood the oak for the new sills afterwards.
endings.text: The place is smaller for a generation, and some names on the sticks have nobody left to pay them. Your oak is in three houses. Nobody thanks you twice, and nobody forgets.
endings.reward: A plot on the rebuilt ground at half its price; Ansgard friendly; a share in the first season's toll forgiven by the church.

endings.how: Came after the fire with a full hold and sold at the price of a burned place.
endings.text: Everything is wanted and you have it. Ansgard pays what you ask, cuts the stick deep, and hangs it where every skipper can see whose mark is on it.
endings.reward: One very good sale (silver, as a good voyage); Ansgard cool to the house, and her granddaughters remember why.

stories.reward: A friend across four generations of one house, or a plot on the new ground, or silver and a long memory against you.

stories.title: A Life for the feast
stories.summary: The priest Hildulf serves Willibrord's church and has no book about Willibrord. Alcuin has written the saint's Life for his kinsman, the abbot of Echternach; the school at Traiectum has it, and a copy can be had for parchment and patience. Hildulf wants to read from it on the saint's day, at the start of winter.
stories.picture: A dark little timber church with one lamp lit: a thin priest holding a small plain book open in both hands as if it were hot, and a merchant in a sea cloak standing in the doorway with rain behind him.

beats.text: Hildulf shows you the chest: the leaf of 726, a psalter with a split spine, and room. He has saved thirty pennies from the church's third. A copy of the Life will cost more than that, and he knows it.

Einold, who taught Hildulf his letters, hears what his old pupil wants and is cross that he was not asked first. Saint Bavo's has no Life of Willibrord. He offers a quire of clean leaves toward the copy, and wants to read it on its way down river.
The schoolmaster at Traiectum has the Life and boys who need the practice. He will have it copied by Michaelmas for a bundle of good calfskin and the price of the ink, and asks who it is for, twice.

Parchment is to be had on the Rhine by the bundle, sixty pennies in a fair year. The clerk Hrotbert hears what you are buying it for and offers a hundred and twenty pennies for the finished book, no questions.
You come up on the flood in the dark days before the saint's feast. Hildulf has lit both lamps on credit. He reads the first leaf aloud to an empty church and then cannot go on for a while.

endings.how: Carried the copy to Andoverpis and took Hildulf's thirty pennies, or nothing.
endings.text: The Life is read on the feast every year after. Hildulf writes your house's name on the last leaf, under the scribe's, and tells the toll man that the church's third is not to be asked of you again.
endings.reward: The church's third of the toll forgiven the house at Andoverpis for good (a third less toll here); lodging and sanctuary at the church; the thread's flag bk_carried; Hildulf a fast friend.

endings.how: Sold the finished book to the clerk at Colonia.
endings.text: A hundred and twenty pennies in the hand. At Andoverpis the second lamp stays dark; Hildulf thanks you for your trouble, and counts your boat in from the church door every time after.
endings.reward: 120 d and the thread's flag bk_knows_worth; Hildulf cool; the toll at Andoverpis is never counted light for this house.

endings.how: Had Beornwine read the book aloud at anchor on the way, and delivered it late and a little salt-stained.
endings.text: The crew know Willibrord's voyages better than most priests. Hildulf turns the stained leaf over twice and says a book that has been to sea is the right book for this church.
endings.reward: As 'given', and the crew's hearts lift on every later feast of Willibrord; the book's worth is known to the house (bk_knows_worth).

stories.reward: A third less toll at Andoverpis for good and a priest who reads for the house, or a hundred and twenty pennies.

stories.title: Thin ale
stories.summary: The grain failed in 792 and stood false in the ear in 793; Andoverpis has pigs and no bread, and Ermentrud is brewing thin. A boatload of barley or rye sold on this bank at the king's price, or over it, is remembered by a house that keeps every stick.
stories.picture: The inside of a big timber house by firelight: a large woman with a ladle looking into a nearly empty vat, thin children on the benches, and through the open door a small boat on the werf with grain sacks in her.

beats.text: Ermentrud brews thin and says so. Poor people from up river sit along her wall and are given broth. She will pay in salt pork, in silver, or on a stick, for malt or barley, and asks what grain costs where you came from.

Up river the cellarer of Saint Peter's has silver and no grain to sell: he is buying next year's wool with it from people who would rather have bread. He says a boat of barley on this river would be remembered longer than a boat of wax, and by more people.
The herdsmen have pigs to sell and nothing to fatten them on: young pigs go at seven pennies a head where ten is asked in a good year. Pork keeps in salt. Salt is at Walichrum.

On the Rhine the king's own grain is sold under his price, from the summer of 794 by a rule: wheat at three pennies the measure, rye at two, barley at one. A dealer offers more, quietly, for anything delivered where no steward looks. The steward Wido has barley marked for the Scheldt and no hull to send it in.
You open the sacks on the selling bank. The priest has come down from the church to watch the measure; the toll man has his hand out; Ermentrud stands at the front and waits to hear the price.

endings.how: Sold grain here at or under the king's price (the thread's flag hy_fed_poor).
endings.text: Ermentrud brews thick for the first time since harvest and the first cup goes to your crew. She cuts no stick for it. The herdsmen bring pigs to your boat's side before they bring them to the bank.
endings.reward: Pigs and salt pork at the herdsman's price here for good (buy at source); Ermentrud a fast friend; the crew's hearts lift; standing with the Franks of the region.

endings.how: Sold at what a hungry place would bear (the thread's flag hy_sold_dear).
endings.text: It is all sold by the turn of the tide. Ermentrud pays, cuts the stick very deep and hangs it by the door. The priest says the feast's prayer for those who sell bread, and looks at nobody.
endings.reward: Silver, half as much again as the king's price; Ermentrud and Hildulf cool; her house remembers it against the heirs.

endings.how: Had no grain, but carried the cheap pigs' meat to Walichrum for salt and brought the salt back.
endings.text: Nobody is fed bread by it, but the pigs that would have starved are in barrels, and the herdsmen have silver for seed corn. Ermentrud says it is the first clever thing a skipper has done here all year.
endings.reward: A standing trade: salt pork down, sea salt up, a good small profit each autumn; Ermentrud friendly; Unno on the island knows the house.

stories.reward: The ale-wife's friendship and pork at source, or a hard profit and a stick by the door.

stories.title: Stag heads
stories.summary: Liafgrim makes the best combs on the Scheldt and never has enough antler: this open country has few stags left. He will pay in combs, which sell for more the further north they go, and to a merchant who keeps him supplied he will give something better than combs.
stories.picture: A lean-to in summer light: stag skulls hanging in a row from a rail, a fair-haired man astride a bench sawing a tine, and a boy beside him holding a half-made comb up to the sun to see through the teeth.

beats.text: Liafgrim offers a dozen combs for a bundle of stag antler, where the bundle cost you six pennies and the dozen sells here for twelve. He says it is a bargain for you. He is right, and it is a better one for him.

Liafgrim will cut antler with no saw but one from the smiths' row at Colonia. Bero has the new blade wrapped and waiting each spring, takes nothing for it but the comb that comes back, and asks, for once, where a thing of his is going.

At the house doors of Ganda the abbeys' tenants buy Liafgrim's plain combs by the piece, and the abbeys' huntsmen have what he never has enough of: shed antler from the abbeys' woods, sold by the bundle to whoever asks first.
The brooch-maker on the island sells Liafgrim's combs beside his own pins, and says a comb in a riveted case with a pattern cut in it fetches double among Danes. He has the rivets.
Liafgrim coughs longer each spring. He asks, without looking up, whether there is a boy in your house or your crew with still hands and nothing to inherit.
Liafgrim does not come with the swallows. If he had a pupil, the lean-to is in use and the stag skulls are hanging; if not, Ermentrud's granddaughter has swept up the dust and kept the bench.

endings.how: Kept him in antler for several summers and left him a boy to teach.
endings.text: The boy can cut teeth by his second Martinmas. When Liafgrim stops coming, the lean-to is the house's own: combs with your mark scratched under the plate go north every summer.
endings.reward: A craftsman's booth here that is the house's own (combs each summer at the cost of the antler); the mark known at the northern sea markets; Liafgrim's saw.

endings.how: Carried combs and Wilbraht's rivets between the two hearths and sold cased combs north.
endings.text: Neither craftsman will say the cased comb was your idea. Both make them for you first, before the big Frisian's men come round.
endings.reward: Cased combs at the maker's price at Andoverpis and Walichrum (a good cargo for the Danish markets: small, light, dear); Liafgrim and Wilbraht friendly; Thiadbod's notice.

endings.how: Let Thiadbod's men buy the whole summer's combs, for a finder's share.
endings.text: Liafgrim takes the price for the lot and works to the count like a man filling sacks. He greets you civilly. He does not ask about the boy again.
endings.reward: A share of silver each Martinmas while Liafgrim lives; Thiadbod easy; no combs at source for this house.

stories.reward: A booth and a mark of the house's own, or the cased combs first, or a share from the rival.

stories.title: Inside or outside
stories.summary: By the count of Flanders's wars the old ale-house stands outside a wall. Ground inside is the margrave's and dear; ground outside is cheap, and in 1055 the Flemings cannot take the castle and burn every house round it. Where the house keeps its goods on this bank is a choice with a date on it.
stories.picture: A grey stone wall with timber houses crowded against its foot, some burning; on the river a line of ships with painted shields; a white-haired woman walking calmly in at the gate with a leather case of sticks under her arm.

beats.text: Gerburg says a plot inside the wall costs four times a plot outside, and that she is a woman who did not buy inside. She asks where your goods lie. The margrave's clerk is asking the same of everyone.
A plot inside is the margrave's to give: silver, a gift first, and an oath to stand a stretch of the wall when the horn blows. He is seldom here; his clerk takes the gift either way.
At Ganda the count's men buy rope, pitch and oars and say nothing of what for. Twice now the march has been named in the ale-houses there as a thing owed to Flanders.

In the count's timber castle on the Leie, Baldwin asks a merchant who trades on both banks what stands outside the wall at Andoverpis and what inside. He asks it pleasantly, as a man asks the price of wool, and remembers the answer.
This year the Flemings besiege the duke in the castle and cannot take it. Every roof outside the wall burns. What was stored inside is whole; what was stored outside is ash, unless it was moved.
The houses outside are up again within the year, Gerburg's first. She has the sticks. She wants to know whether your house will lend her the price of a roof, and on what terms.

endings.how: Bought a plot inside the wall and swore to the stretch before 1055.
endings.text: The house's goods come through the siege untouched, and one of your men stands on the wall for nine days eating the margrave's bread. Afterwards the toll house reads your charter quickly.
endings.reward: The plot and its stores safe in every later raid on the place; standing with the margrave's men; the toll asked without search.

endings.how: Heard the talk at Ganda and brought it to Gerburg in time.
endings.text: Her casks, her vat and her sticks are inside the gate two days before the ships come. The roof burns anyway. She rebuilds on your loan and pays it back in three years, to the day.
endings.reward: Gerburg a fast friend, and her house the house's factor on this bank: she buys and stores for you at her own price; the loan back with a gift.

endings.how: Kept the goods outside the wall, where storage was cheap, and was elsewhere in 1055.
endings.text: Ash, and a few hoops. Gerburg carried out what she could of yours with her own, which was one cask and the tally of the rest.
endings.reward: The stored goods lost; the tally of them, which the margrave's clerk will hear as a suit against nobody; Gerburg friendly, for she tried.

stories.reward: Goods that outlast the siege and the margrave's good word, or a factor for life on the Scheldt, or a lesson with a date.

works.name: A corner of the ale-house loft
works.what: Room under the thatch of the house on posts for a few casks and bales, with the ale-wife's eye on them and a stick cut for the count.
works.needs: The ale-wife at least easy with you.
works.gives: Store up to six units at Andoverpis between calls. Nothing stored here is safe in 836 or in 1055 unless it was moved first.
works.picture: A dim loft under thatch: three casks and a bale against a great post, a split tally stick stuck in the wattle above them.
works.source: works_793.json store_corner; the house from Bellens 2021; the loft is ours

works.name: A well with grooved posts
works.what: A square timber well sunk by the path from the werf: four oak corner posts with grooves cut down them and planks slid in from above, a hand and a half wide inside. Sweet water where the river is brackish on a spring tide.
works.needs: Leave of the priest or the toll man, since it is dug on common ground.
works.gives: Taking on water here costs no time, for you and every boat; the people of the place speak well of the house; a fire near it takes less.
works.picture: A square hole in sandy ground lined with planks between four grooved posts, a leather bucket on a rope, a woman and a skipper both waiting to draw.
works.source: Bellens 2021: a square timber well of the 9th century, 60 cm inside, planks slid into grooved corner posts; works_793.json well

works.name: Incense and lights for Peter and Paul
works.what: Oil and wax for the second lamp for a year, and a pound of incense for the feasts, as the giver of 726 asked and nobody since has paid for. The priest names the house in his prayers at Mass.
works.needs: A pound of incense carried here, or its price; the priest's good will.
works.gives: Standing with the Christians of the port rises (the deed gave_alms, counted well); the house's name is said at the altar; the priest reads and writes for the house without a fee.
works.picture: Two hanging lamps both lit before a plain altar, a thread of incense smoke, and a priest looking up at the second lamp with his mouth a little open.
works.source: The charter of 726: the gift is 'for incense and lights' and for the priests' prayers for the givers (Mertens and Torfs I, 1845); goods_793.json incense and wax

works.name: A log path to the werf
works.what: Split logs laid crosswise on long bearers from the foot of the bank down to the landing, a pace wide, with wood chips trodden in between: dry going for porters at any state of the mud.
works.needs: Oak or alder floated down for it; the wright's time.
works.gives: Loading takes half the time here for every ship, and the selling bank is fuller in the wet months; standing with the householders.
works.picture: A road of pale split logs running from a grass bank down across brown mud to a grounded boat, a porter with a cask on his shoulder walking it dry-shod.
works.source: Bellens 2021: corduroy paths of split logs on long bearers, 1.5 m and 1 m wide, along the rampart's inner foot in the 10th century, wood chips on the paths; works_793.json causeway. That one ran to the landing is ours

works.name: A long plot inside the bank
works.what: A narrow strip of ground inside the half ring, short end to the path, with room for a wattle house on oak posts and a store behind it. It comes with a stretch of the bank to keep and to stand on.
works.needs: Known in the port; from about 974 the margrave's leave and a gift first.
works.gives: The house may build its own works here (storehouse, cellar, booth); what lies on the plot is safe when the houses outside burn in 1055; the house counts as a householder in a suit.
works.picture: Seen from the top of a grass bank: long narrow fenced strips side by side, each with a wattle house end-on to a log path, smoke from every roof, one strip still bare with pegs and cord marking it out.
works.source: Bellens 2021: long narrow plots of the 10th century, houses 5 to 7 m wide with the short end to the street, wattle of hazel and willow on oak posts; works_793.json plot. The duty on the bank is ours (?)

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: The boats of the place: for the creeks, the nets and the mud of the inlets. The carpenters build one between Martinmas and Easter, partly from planks that have been a boat before.
ships.picture: A small open boat half planked on trestles beside a muddy inlet, old grey strakes and new yellow ones in the same hull.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json west_small_boat; carpenters and reused ship's timber from Bellens 2021. No boat has been found here: the building is ours

ships.note: Flat boats work the Schijn ferry and the reed beds. The ferryman has an old one to sell most years, and it serves as a lighter when she must lie off the werf.
ships.picture: A flat punt on a rope across a brown creek mouth, a pole stuck upright in the mud beside her.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json skiff_punt; the ferry at the Schijn mouth (nl.wikipedia Geschiedenis van Antwerpen)

ships.note: The one sea-going kind seen at the werf: a beach-landing boat that carries the abbeys' goods between the islands, this bank and Ganda. One is for sale when an abbey's steward wants silver more than a hull.
ships.picture: A broad beamy boat grounded upright on the sand point at low water, her mast stepped, a monk and a skipper walking round her.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json coaster_minster_ship; traffic_793.json gives Andoverpis one coaster; Ganda's abbey boats (dossier of Ganda)

ships.note: Barges bring white pots from the Maas, red-painted pots from the Rhine and, after 1000, stone from Tournai. Bargemen who have sold their load sell the barge too, sooner than haul her back against the stream.
ships.picture: A long flat barge lying empty under a turf bank, chips of grey stone still in her bottom, a hauling rope coiled on the bow.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json river_barge; Bellens 2021: Meuse and Rhenish wares about half of all sherds in the 10th century, Tournai stone by the Scheldt

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: With a margrave, a wall and wrights who have built in oak all their lives, a sea-going hull can be ordered here in the march's years, if the oak is found: this country grows few trees, and it is floated down from the south.
ships.picture: A big round-hulled ship in frame on the bank below a grey wall, oak logs rafted in the inlet beside her.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json north_sea_merchant_ship; the place flowers in the 10th and 11th centuries (Bellens 2021); open country with few trees (Bellens). No yard is known: ours (?)

sayings.text: Whoever breaks this gift, let him have the lot of Judas, and of Ananias and Sapphira, and the leprosy of Gehazi; and let him pay the king's treasury two pounds of gold and five of silver.
sayings.source: The curse of the charter of 20 October 726, after the Dutch of Mertens and Torfs I (1845), pp. 74-75 (our rendering; the Latin not read). The toll man says it to anyone who argues about the church's third

sayings.text: This year the Northmen burned Andwerpa, and likewise Witla.
sayings.source: Annales Fuldenses 836 (Latin, our rendering), in the Chronicle's manner. Said afterwards to date anything: 'two winters before the year the Northmen burned us'

sayings.text: Have the Frank for your friend, but not for your neighbor.
sayings.source: A Greek proverb in Einhard, Life of Charles 16 (tr. S. E. Turner 1880), as given in Design/content/peoples/frankish.md 8. Said here, after 925, of the count of Flanders across the river

sayings.text: A new toll is a robbery; an old one is the weather.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, on the rule of Thionville (805) that only old tolls are lawful

sayings.text: I grew on a proud head and I go through humbler ones. What the stag threw away, the king's daughter wears. Say what I am.
sayings.source: invented in the manner of the Exeter riddles (the answer: a comb); not a quotation

sayings.text: The river gave the ground, and the river is owed for it.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, on the name: probably 'at the thrown-up ground', silted land in a river bend (nl.wikipedia Antwerpen (stad))

sayings.text: Nobody here keeps a horse. A pig eats what a horse would and you can eat the pig.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; hardly a horse bone in the digs, pig bones 46 in a hundred before 980 (Bellens 2021)

easter_eggs.text: In the church's chest, under the leaf of 726, lies a very small gold piece with a head on one side and the letters ANDERPVS round it. The priest says it is the only thing in the place with the place's name on it, and that nobody strikes gold now.
easter_eggs.source: Tremisses of the moneyer Chrodigisilus reading ANDERPVS, about 650 (Bellens 2021; nl.wikipedia Geschiedenis van Antwerpen). That one lies in the chest is ours

easter_eggs.text: One plank of the ale-house wall is curved and has a row of old rivet holes along it. In every later house on that ground there is such a plank.
easter_eggs.source: Van de Walle noted reused ship's timber in the oldest houses he dug (Bellens 2021)

easter_eggs.text: When the bank is thrown up, a small worn bronze coin with a strange king's head turns up in the spoil and is shovelled back in.
easter_eggs.source: A coin of the emperor Constans (348-350, struck at Trier) was found in the rampart (Bellens 2021)

easter_eggs.text: The toll man always holds out his open hand before he speaks, and says a false oath costs a man the hand he swore with. Nobody on this bank has lost one. Stories grow in places like this.
easter_eggs.source: The law is real: a perjurer 'shall lose his right hand' (capitulary of 802 c. 36, Henderson 1892). The tale of the giant who cut off skippers' hands at this toll is first written in the 15th century (nl.wikipedia Silvius Brabo) and is not in the game

easter_eggs.text: Every furrow in the dark fields turns up red potsherds, worn smooth. The children call them 'old men's bread' and skim them on the river.
easter_eggs.source: The dark layer of grey sand full of worn Roman sherds, and Roman tile built into later houses (Bellens 2021). The children's name is ours

easter_eggs.text: The priest can tell you that the man who gave this church away had it by swapping a whole hamlet, Tumme, to an abbot for it; and that nobody now knows where Tumme was.
easter_eggs.source: Rauchingus had the church by exchange from Firminus, abbot of 'Quortolodra', for his hamlet Tumme (charter of 726, Mertens and Torfs I)

easter_eggs.text: A hunter on the selling bank has a beaver's pelt for sale and the tail with it, which he says is fish and may be eaten in Lent.
easter_eggs.source: Beaver bones among the game (Bellens 2021). That beaver tail counts as fish on fast days is a later medieval saying, unchecked for these years (?)

unlocks.what: The church's third of the toll forgiven the house at Andoverpis
unlocks.how: End 'A Life for the feast' by bringing the priest the book (the endings 'given' or 'read aboard').
unlocks.gives: toll at Andoverpis a third less for this house, inherited; act:lodge and act:sanctuary at the church; the thread's flag bk_carried.

unlocks.what: A tally stick in the ale-house with nothing cut on it
unlocks.how: End 'The sticks first' by bringing warning before the fleet of 836.
unlocks.gives: npc alewife feeling carries undiminished to her heirs and yours: free lodging and storage here until 1066, and in 1022-1062 Gerburg greets the house by its mark.

unlocks.what: Pigs and salt pork at the herdsman's price
unlocks.how: End 'Thin ale' by selling grain here at or under the king's price in a hungry year (792-794, 805-807).
unlocks.gives: buy_at_source for pigs and salt_pork at Andoverpis; the thread's flag hy_fed_poor.

unlocks.what: Combs with the house's own mark
unlocks.how: End 'Stag heads' with a pupil at the comb-maker's bench.
unlocks.gives: A booth of the house's own here: a dozen combs each summer for a bundle of antler; standing word at the northern sea markets where the mark is known.

unlocks.what: A householder's standing inside the wall
unlocks.how: Buy the long plot inside the bank and swear to its stretch (the story 'Inside or outside', ending 'inside').
unlocks.gives: Stored goods here are untouched in 1055; in a lawsuit at the margrave's hall the house's odds are one word better.

unlocks.what: Gerburg's house as the house's factor on the Scheldt
unlocks.how: End 'Inside or outside' by carrying the talk of Ganda to her before the siege and lending for her roof.
unlocks.gives: A factor at Andoverpis who buys in the cheap season and stores for the house; commission between Andoverpis and Ganda each year.

The editor's pass of 7 October 2026. The king's own grain at Frankfurt in 794 is oats two measures a penny, barley one penny, rye two, wheat three; the top price for other men's is one, two, three and four (Synod of Frankfurt c. 4, MGH Capitularia I no. 28, as in chronicle_793.json 794-06-01-frankfurt-prices). The bank of 13.5 m and the paths of 1.5 m (Bellens 2021) are given in paces of about a metre and a half. Blood-month and Lammas are English names; a Frank says before Advent and Saint Peter's Chains (1 August).

Not checked, and marked (?) where used: the Latin of the charter of 726 (Wampach, Echternach no. 34); whether Echternach still held the church in 793; the date of Alcuin's Life of Willibrord; any visit of Gothelo to the place; D.
